text: Whenever you count things, orders returned, tickets received, visitors who convert, the counts tend to follow one of a few standard shapes. A distribution is simply a rule that gives the probability of each possible outcome. In this lesson we meet the four discrete ones you will use most.

Bernoulli is a single yes or no trial with success probability p. Binomial counts the successes across n such trials. Poisson counts events in a fixed window of time when they arrive independently at a steady average rate. Geometric counts how many trials it takes to get the first success.

Say ten orders ship today and each has a thirty percent chance of being returned. In scipy, stats dot binom of ten and point three gives an object. Its pmf at three is about zero point two six seven, the chance of exactly three returns. The cdf at three is about zero point six five, three or fewer. And the survival function at four is about zero point one five, the chance of five or more.

Never trust a formula you cannot verify. Simulate a hundred thousand days with numpy and count how often exactly three returns happen. You get point two six seven nine, close to the exact point two six six eight. A simulation always carries a little random noise, so expect close, not identical.

Now suppose a help desk averages four tickets an hour. Poisson says a completely silent hour happens under two percent of the time, and eight or more tickets in an hour about five percent of the time. A telltale Poisson feature is that the mean and the variance are equal. If your real counts vary much more than their average, Poisson is the wrong model.
All of this rests on assumptions, mainly that trials are independent and the probability stays constant. Check them honestly. Up next is the most famous distribution of all: the normal distribution.
